title: Character Streams: FileReader and FileWriter
learningObjectives: Read text data through character-oriented Reader APIs
Write text using character-oriented Writer implementations
Explain why a runtime default charset may reduce portability
Select explicit UTF-8 APIs for consistent cross-platform text
Handle checked I/O failures when reading or writing character data

understand.concept: FileReader and FileWriter are character-oriented APIs. Their default charset depends on runtime configuration; portable applications should choose an explicit Charset such as UTF-8.
understand.whyItMatters: Character streams convert between bytes and characters using a charset. Making the encoding explicit avoids platform-dependent text corruption when files move between operating systems or contain characters outside basic ASCII.
understand.analogy: A character stream is like two people agreeing on the same alphabet and codebook before exchanging a written message.
understand.analogyLimit: Java char represents a UTF-16 code unit, not always one complete Unicode code point or one user-perceived symbol. A charset also defines byte encoding, not visual rendering.

explain.narrative:
## Character streams represent text

`Reader` and `Writer` are character-oriented abstractions. They let a program process text as characters rather than manually managing raw bytes. `FileReader` reads characters from a file and `FileWriter` writes characters to a file, but their convenience constructors use the runtime's default charset.

## Make encoding explicit

A text file is still stored as bytes. A charset defines how those bytes map to characters. If an application must exchange files predictably across machines, choose the charset explicitly, commonly UTF-8. Use `Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)` and `Files.newBufferedWriter(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`, or an `InputStreamReader`/`OutputStreamWriter` with an explicit charset.

## Avoid mismatched decoding

A file written as UTF-8 must be decoded as UTF-8. Reading those bytes with a different charset can produce mojibake or replacement characters. ASCII-only examples may hide this bug because many encodings represent basic Latin characters identically.

## Buffering, ownership and tests

For larger files, use buffered readers and writers to reduce repeated low-level operations. Use try-with-resources for streams your code owns; closing a reader or writer releases its underlying resource. Test accented characters and non-Latin scripts, an empty file, a final line without a newline and an I/O failure. Verify the decoded text exactly rather than checking only that the file exists.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var reader = new java.io.StringReader("Java")) { System.out.println((char)reader.read()); } } }
examples.explanation: Reads a character from a character stream.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var writer = new java.io.StringWriter()) { writer.write("Java IO"); System.out.println(writer.toString()); } } }

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8.name()); } }
examples.explanation: Selects an explicit charset for portable text.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var reader = new java.io.StringReader("ABC")) { System.out.println(reader.read()); } } }
examples.explanation: The first character A has numeric code point value 65 in this example.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var writer = new java.io.StringWriter()) { writer.append("File").append("Writer"); System.out.println(writer); } } }
examples.explanation: Shows chained character writes to a Writer.

practise.guidedTask: Write text using a character writer and read it back using UTF-8-aware APIs. Explain why the charset must be agreed by both sides.
practise.independentTask: Compare FileReader/FileWriter defaults with Files.newBufferedReader/newBufferedWriter using StandardCharsets.UTF_8.
hints: FileReader/FileWriter convenience constructors use a default charset; choose an explicit charset when file interchange must be predictable.
Use the same charset for writing and reading; ASCII-only tests may conceal an encoding mismatch.
Test accented and non-Latin text, empty input and I/O failures; use buffering for larger files.
practise.challenge: Test non-ASCII text such as café and Telugu characters, then verify the decoded text exactly matches the original.

questions.prompt: What is the main distinction between character streams and byte streams?
options: Character streams read/write text characters; byte streams handle raw bytes
Byte streams automatically parse Java source
questions.answer: Character streams read/write text characters; byte streams handle raw bytes
questions.explanation: Byte streams transfer raw bytes; Reader and Writer APIs operate on decoded characters for text processing.

questions.prompt: What risk comes from relying on a default charset?
options: The same file may be interpreted differently across environments
questions.answer: The same file may be interpreted differently across environments
questions.explanation: A runtime-dependent default charset can differ between machines, so the same bytes may be decoded into different text.

questions.prompt: Which API lets an application specify a charset when reading a file?
questions.explanation: Files.newBufferedReader accepts an explicit Charset, making the decoding contract clear and portable.

questions.prompt: Which class is a character-oriented file writer?
questions.explanation: FileWriter is a character-oriented file writer; use an explicit charset API when the encoding must be predictable.

questions.prompt: Why should text encoding be explicit for cross-platform data exchange?
options: Both writer and reader need a consistent character-to-byte mapping
It guarantees the text is grammatically correct
questions.answer: Both writer and reader need a consistent character-to-byte mapping
questions.explanation: Using the same documented charset on both sides ensures characters are encoded into and decoded from bytes consistently.
